why_how.text: Alcohol slows judgment and reaction long before a driver feels drunk, so risk climbs even below the legal limit.
North Carolina uses one offense, DWI, and it can be proven by impairment or by a BAC number.

scenario.text: Dana is pulled over after two drinks, and a test shows a BAC of zero point zero six while driving a car.

reasoning.text: Zero point zero six is below the car per se level, but crash risk already rises from zero point zero five, and DWI can also be proven by appreciable impairment.

result.text: If an officer shows Dana's faculties were appreciably impaired, Dana can still be found guilty of DWI.

claim.text: Many people think zero point zero five is the legal limit for a car driver.

correction.text: Zero point zero five is where crash risk starts to rise; the per se limit for a car driver is zero point zero eight.

memory_support.text: Five is risk, eight is law.

prompt.text: Dana drives a car with a BAC of zero point zero six, and her faculties are clearly impaired. Can DWI be proven?

answer.text: Yes, by showing appreciable impairment of her faculties.

rationale.text: DWI can be proven either by appreciable impairment or by a BAC at the per se level, so being under the number is not a defense.

narration.text: This chapter is about alcohol and driving, one of the most heavily tested topics in any driver handbook. This first lesson builds the foundation. You will learn what blood alcohol concentration, or BAC, measures, the level at which every driver is impaired, the lower level where crash risk begins to climb, how North Carolina folded its drunk-driving laws into one offense called Driving While Impaired, the two ways that offense can be proven, the stricter limit for commercial drivers, and the roadblocks officers may use. Keep the numbers straight from the start, because the practice questions certainly will test them.

lines.text: Every driver impaired at point oh eight.
Crash risk rises at point oh five.

narration.text: Blood alcohol concentration measures how much alcohol is in your blood. At a BAC of zero point zero eight percent, every driver is impaired, and many people are affected at far lower levels. Crash risk begins rising at a BAC of zero point zero five percent, and at zero point zero eight percent the chance of causing a fatal crash is greater still. So impairment is not a switch that flips at one number. It builds as BAC climbs, and the earliest effects, slower reactions and weaker judgment, show up before most drivers feel any different. The safest choice is not to drive after drinking at all.

lines.text: Point oh five: crash risk rises.
Point oh eight: car driver limit.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two numbers sit close together, and only one of them is a legal limit for a car driver. The zero point zero five figure is where crash risk starts to rise. It is not a legal limit. The legal per se limit for a car driver is zero point zero eight. Practice questions often offer zero point zero five as the limit, and it is tempting because it sounds cautious. Do not take it. Hold the memory line instead: five is risk, eight is law. Commercial drivers have their own lower limit, which comes up in a moment.

lines.text: Safe Roads Act replaced older laws.
A single offense: Driving While Impaired.

narration.text: North Carolina simplified its drunk-driving laws with the Safe Roads Act of nineteen eighty-three. That act replaced all the earlier drunk-driving laws with a single offense called Driving While Impaired, known as DWI. Whether the cause is alcohol, drugs, or both, the charge is the same offense. Having one offense means the rules about testing, revocation and penalties all connect to the same charge, which is why the rest of this chapter keeps returning to DWI. When a practice question mentions drunk driving in North Carolina, the legal name you should have in mind is Driving While Impaired.

lines.text: Or a BAC at the per se level.

narration.text: DWI can be proven in two separate ways. The first is by showing that alcohol, drugs or both appreciably impaired the driver's physical or mental faculties. No number is needed for this route; the evidence is how the person was driving and behaving. The second is by a BAC of zero point zero eight percent or more, or zero point zero four or more when driving a commercial motor vehicle. Either route is enough on its own. So a driver below the BAC number can still be convicted if impairment is shown, and a driver at the number is guilty even if they feel fine.

lines.text: Commercial vehicle limit: point oh four.

narration.text: The per se DWI limit is zero point zero eight for an ordinary driver, but zero point zero four for a driver of a commercial motor vehicle. The lower commercial limit reflects the weight, the passengers and the cargo those vehicles carry. A practice question that describes a truck or bus driver and asks about the BAC limit wants the commercial figure. Enforcement has tools too. North Carolina DWI laws allow law enforcement to set up roadblocks to check for impaired drivers, so a checkpoint on a busy weekend night is a lawful part of the system, not an unusual event.

lines.text: BAC of point oh six in a car.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Dana is driving a car, and a test shows a BAC of zero point zero six, below the car per se level. But the officer also documents that her speech, balance and driving show her faculties were appreciably impaired. Can DWI be proven? Work it out before reading on. The answer is yes. DWI can be proven by showing that alcohol, drugs or both appreciably impaired the driver's faculties, so being under the per se number is not a defense. The BAC route and the impairment route are separate, and either one is enough.

lines.text: Five is risk, eight is law.

narration.text: Let us pull it together. Every driver is impaired at a BAC of zero point zero eight, and crash risk already begins rising at zero point zero five, which is a risk level, not a legal limit. The Safe Roads Act replaced earlier laws with one offense, Driving While Impaired. DWI is proven by appreciable impairment from alcohol, drugs or both, or by a BAC of zero point zero eight or more, or zero point zero four or more in a commercial vehicle. And officers may use roadblocks to check for impaired drivers. Next, the chemical test and what refusing it costs.

why_how.text: The chemical test turns suspicion into evidence, so refusing it carries penalties of its own.
A high result costs your privilege immediately, before any court date, to get an impaired driver off the road.

scenario.text: Riley is charged with DWI and refuses the breath test, hoping no number means no case.

reasoning.text: Refusing brings an immediate revocation of at least thirty days and a further DMV revocation of at least twelve months, and the refusal can be used in court.

result.text: Riley ends up with a longer revocation than a failed test would have brought, plus evidence of refusal in court.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking that refusing the chemical test is a safe way to avoid a revocation.

correction.text: Refusing brings at least thirty days immediately plus at least twelve months from DMV, which is more than the thirty days for failing.

prompt.text: Riley refuses the breath test after a DWI charge. Which revocations follow?

answer.text: At least thirty days immediately, then at least twelve months from DMV.

rationale.text: Refusal carries both revocations, and the refusal itself can also be used as evidence in court.

lines.text: Asked of drivers charged with DWI.
Refusing or failing both cost you.

narration.text: When a driver is charged with DWI, the next step is usually a chemical test. This lesson covers what that test is, what happens if you refuse it, what happens if you fail it, how a limited driving privilege can sometimes follow a refusal, and how both results and refusals are treated in court. Many people believe refusing the test is a clever way out. The handbook makes clear it is not. Refusal carries its own penalties, and those penalties are actually heavier than the immediate revocation that follows a failed test. Let us walk through each piece in order.

lines.text: Results and refusals used in court.

narration.text: A driver charged with DWI will be asked to take a chemical test of breath or blood. The test measures alcohol concentration, which is one of the two ways DWI can be proven. Both your chemical test result and any refusal to be tested can be used as evidence in court. That second point surprises people. Refusing does not erase the question of impairment; it simply adds a new piece of evidence, the refusal itself, while the officer's observations of your driving and behavior still count. So the test request is a turning point, and every choice at that moment has consequences.

lines.text: Immediate revocation: at least thirty days.
DMV revocation: at least twelve months.
Limited privilege possible after six months.

narration.text: Refusing a required chemical test brings an immediate license revocation of at least thirty days, and then a further DMV revocation of at least twelve months. In some cases, once six months of a willful-refusal revocation have passed, a judge may grant a limited driving privilege, which allows driving for specific purposes under conditions. But that relief is not automatic, and it only comes after half a year without driving. So a refusal does not save a license. It locks in a long revocation, on top of whatever happens with the DWI charge itself in court.

lines.text: Car driver: point oh eight or more.
Commercial driver: point oh four or more.
Revoked immediately, at least thirty days.

narration.text: A test result of zero point zero eight or more, or zero point zero four or more in a commercial motor vehicle, means your driving privilege is revoked immediately for at least thirty days. The word immediately matters. This revocation happens right away, before any trial, as a safety measure to keep an impaired driver off the road. The court case on the DWI charge continues separately, and a conviction brings its own revocation later. So a failed test sets off two tracks: the immediate revocation now, and the possible conviction penalties that the following lessons describe.

lines.text: Refusing: thirty days plus twelve months.

narration.text: Here is the trap, and it is an important one. Refusing the chemical test brings at least thirty days of immediate revocation plus at least twelve months from DMV, while failing it at zero point zero eight or more brings an immediate revocation of at least thirty days. So the refusal path is the longer one, by a full year or more. Practice questions sometimes describe refusal as the lighter choice, or say the twelve-month revocation follows a failed test. Both are backwards. The memory line keeps it simple: refusal adds a year, and the refusal can still be used against you in court.

Here is a quick check: Riley is charged with DWI and refuses the breath test, thinking that without a number there can be no case. Which revocations follow from the refusal? Work it out before reading on. The answer is an immediate revocation of at least thirty days, followed by a DMV revocation of at least twelve months. In some cases a judge may grant a limited privilege after six months, but not before. And Riley's refusal can be used as evidence in court, alongside the officer's observations. Refusing made Riley's situation longer, not shorter.

To wrap up, a driver charged with DWI is asked to take a chemical test of breath or blood, and both the result and any refusal can be used in court. Refusing brings an immediate revocation of at least thirty days plus a DMV revocation of at least twelve months, with a possible limited privilege after six months in some cases. A result of zero point zero eight or more, or zero point zero four or more in a commercial vehicle, revokes the privilege immediately for at least thirty days. Refusing is the longer path. Next, alcohol inside the vehicle.

why_how.text: Drinking while driving and open containers invite impaired driving, so the law bans them outright.
Commercial vehicles carry more risk, so even closed containers are banned in their passenger areas.

scenario.text: A friend riding in the back seat of Lee's car opens a can of beer on the way home from a game.

reasoning.text: Carrying an open container of any alcoholic beverage is prohibited anywhere in the vehicle, including the passenger area.

result.text: Lee pulls over and the friend pours it out, because the open container is not allowed even if Lee is sober.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking open containers are fine as long as only passengers are drinking.

correction.text: Open containers are banned anywhere in a car's passenger area, and in a commercial vehicle's passenger area even closed containers are banned.

prompt.text: Lee is sober, but a back-seat passenger opens a beer. Is that allowed in Lee's car?

answer.text: No. Open containers are banned in the passenger area too.

rationale.text: The open container rule covers the whole vehicle, so passengers cannot carry open alcohol either.

narration.text: This short lesson covers alcohol that is inside the vehicle, rather than inside the driver. North Carolina bans drinking while driving and bans open containers, and it sets an even stricter rule for commercial vehicles. These rules matter because practice questions like to describe a sober driver with a passenger holding a drink, or a commercial driver with an unopened bottle in the cab, and ask whether the situation is legal. By the end of this lesson you should be able to sort those cases quickly, using the difference between an ordinary car and a commercial motor vehicle.

lines.text: No drinking while driving, beer included.
No open container anywhere in the car.

narration.text: Drinking any alcoholic beverage while driving is prohibited, and beer is included. There is no level of drinking behind the wheel that is acceptable. The rule also reaches beyond the driver's own hands. Carrying an open container of any alcoholic beverage in a vehicle is prohibited, including in the passenger area. So a passenger cannot sip a drink while you drive, and an opened bottle cannot ride along on the seat. A sober driver is not a defense here. The open container rule is about the container in the vehicle, whoever is holding it.

lines.text: Passenger area of a commercial vehicle.

narration.text: Commercial motor vehicles have a stricter rule. In the passenger area of a commercial motor vehicle on a public road, alcohol is banned whether the container is open or closed. So even a sealed bottle, still in its bag from the store, is not allowed in that space. The tighter rule matches the tighter BAC limit for commercial drivers that you saw earlier. Commercial vehicles carry passengers, heavy freight and hazardous loads, and the state removes even the temptation of alcohol from the cab and passenger areas of those vehicles while they are on public roads.

lines.text: Commercial vehicle: open or closed banned.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The two container rules sound alike, but they cover different things. An open container is banned anywhere in a car's passenger area, while in a commercial vehicle's passenger area even closed containers are banned. So a sealed six-pack in the back seat of a family car is not an open container violation. The same sealed six-pack in the passenger area of a commercial vehicle on a public road is a violation. Practice questions swap these on purpose. Ask two things: what kind of vehicle is it, and is the container open or closed?

Here is a quick check: Lee is driving friends home from a game and has not had anything to drink. A passenger in the back seat opens a can of beer. Is that allowed in Lee's car? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Carrying an open container of any alcoholic beverage in a vehicle, including in the passenger area, is prohibited, and Lee being sober does not change that. Lee should pull over safely and have the passenger get rid of the open can. Had the can stayed sealed in an ordinary car, the open container rule would not apply.

lines.text: No open containers in a car.
No alcohol in a commercial passenger area.

narration.text: Let us recap. Drinking any alcoholic beverage while driving, beer included, is prohibited. Carrying an open container of any alcoholic beverage in a vehicle is prohibited, including in the passenger area, whoever is holding it and whether or not the driver is sober. In the passenger area of a commercial motor vehicle on a public road, alcohol is banned whether the container is open or closed. So cars ban open containers, and commercial vehicles ban all containers in the passenger area. Next, the penalties that follow a DWI conviction.

why_how.text: Penalties rise with seriousness and with repeat offenses, so a driver's history shapes the punishment.
The law also aims to treat alcohol problems, because punishment alone does not stop repeat offending.

scenario.text: Pat has a DWI conviction from two years ago and is now convicted of a second DWI.

reasoning.text: A second DWI conviction brings a mandatory four-year revocation when the earlier offense happened within three years, and a second conviction requires jail time.

result.text: Pat faces a four-year revocation, jail time, and a substance abuse assessment before reinstatement.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every DWI look-back window is the same length.

correction.text: The windows differ: three years for the second-offense four-year revocation, five years for a permanent third, seven years for the felony fourth.

prompt.text: Pat's earlier DWI offense was two years before a new conviction. What revocation applies to this second conviction?

rationale.text: The second-offense window is three years, and two years falls inside it.

lines.text: Treatment is part of the law.

narration.text: This lesson covers what happens after a DWI conviction. North Carolina's penalties are built in levels, rising with the seriousness of the offense and with how recently a driver was convicted before. The law also aims to help offenders who have alcohol problems, not only to punish them. You will learn the treatment requirements, then the mandatory revocations for a first, second, third and fourth conviction, along with the look-back windows that decide when the harsher penalties apply. The windows are the part practice questions test most, so we will gather them together near the end.

Punishment levels rise with the seriousness of the offense, and a second DWI conviction requires time in jail. Alongside punishment, DWI laws aim to help offenders with alcohol problems. Repeat offenders and drivers with high BAC levels are checked for an alcohol problem, and lower-BAC offenders attend alcohol safety school. One requirement applies to everyone. Anyone convicted of DWI must complete a substance abuse assessment before driving privileges are reinstated. So the path back to driving always runs through an assessment, whatever the level of the offense.

lines.text: Second within three years: four years.

narration.text: Now the revocations. A first DWI conviction brings a mandatory one-year license revocation. Mandatory means the court has no option to skip it. A second DWI conviction brings a mandatory four-year revocation when the earlier offense happened within three years of the current one. So timing matters for the second conviction. A driver whose earlier offense falls inside that three-year window faces four years without a license, plus the jail time a second conviction requires. Notice how quickly the stakes jump, from one year for a first conviction to four years for a recent second.

lines.text: Third, prior within five years: permanent.
Felony if three priors within seven years.

narration.text: A third DWI conviction brings mandatory permanent revocation if at least one earlier conviction happened within the past five years. A fourth DWI conviction brings mandatory permanent revocation, and it is a felony if the three earlier convictions all happened within the past seven years. A felony is a far more serious crime than a misdemeanor, with lasting consequences beyond driving. So by the third and fourth convictions, the question is no longer how long the revocation lasts, but whether the license is gone for good and whether the driver faces a felony.

Here is the trap. Each conviction level has its own look-back window, and the numbers climb in a pattern. Look-back windows differ by conviction: three years for the four-year second-offense revocation, five years for permanent revocation on a third, and seven years for the felony fourth. Practice questions mix them, for example by applying the five-year window to a second conviction, or the seven-year window to a third. Keep the order: second, third, fourth matches three, five, seven. And remember that the first conviction has no window at all; it always brings one year.

lines.text: One year, four years, permanent, felony.

narration.text: It helps to see the whole ladder at once. A first conviction means one year. A second, with the earlier offense within three years, means four years and jail time. A third, with a prior within five years, means permanent revocation. A fourth means permanent revocation and, with three priors in seven years, a felony. At every level, getting driving privileges back requires a substance abuse assessment, and offenders may be checked for alcohol problems or sent to alcohol safety school. The ladder is steep on purpose, so that a first conviction is a strong warning.

Here is a quick check: Pat's earlier DWI offense happened two years before a new DWI conviction. What revocation applies to this second conviction? Work it out before reading on. The answer is a mandatory four-year revocation. The second-offense window is three years, and two years falls inside it. Pat also faces jail time, which a second conviction requires, and must complete a substance abuse assessment before driving privileges can be reinstated. If the earlier offense had been more than three years back, the four-year rule would not apply in that form.

To finish, DWI punishment rises with seriousness, a second conviction requires jail, and the law aims to help as well as punish, with alcohol checks for repeat and high-BAC offenders and alcohol safety school for lower-BAC offenders. Every convicted driver completes a substance abuse assessment before reinstatement. A first conviction brings one year. A second within three years brings four years. A third with a prior within five years is permanent. A fourth is permanent and a felony with three priors in seven years. Next, the restrictions and devices that follow a conviction.

why_how.text: A restored license after DWI carries a BAC restriction so that any drinking before driving is tightly limited.
An ignition interlock physically stops a car from starting after drinking, for the drivers most likely to reoffend.

scenario.text: Morgan's license is being restored for the second time after DWI suspensions.

reasoning.text: The restriction is zero point zero four on the first restoration and zero point zero zero on the second or any later restoration.

result.text: Morgan's restored license carries a zero point zero zero restriction.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every restored license after DWI carries the same zero point zero four restriction.

correction.text: The restriction is zero point zero four only on the first restoration; every later restoration is zero point zero zero.

prompt.text: Morgan's license is restored for the second time after DWI. What BAC restriction applies?

rationale.text: Only the first restoration allows zero point zero four; later restorations are zero.

narration.text: When a driver gets a license back after a DWI, the license does not come back clean. This lesson covers the conditions attached to restored licenses and to limited driving privileges after a DWI conviction. You will learn when a blood alcohol concentration restriction is placed, the levels it takes, the cases where it starts at zero, the convictions that require an ignition interlock device, and the court's power to seize and sell a vehicle when someone drives while already revoked. These rules are designed to make a second offense much harder to commit and much more costly.

lines.text: Placed on a license restored after DWI.
Or on a limited privilege after DWI.

narration.text: A blood alcohol concentration restriction is placed on a license restored after a DWI suspension, or on a Limited Driving Privilege granted after a DWI conviction. The restriction sets a maximum BAC the driver may have while driving, far below the usual per se limit. The restriction is zero point zero four on the first restoration, and zero point zero zero on the second or any later restoration. So the first time a license is restored, a very small amount is tolerated. After that, the tolerance disappears entirely, and any alcohol at all puts the driver in violation of the restriction.

Here is the trap. The restored-license BAC restriction is zero point zero four the first time and zero point zero zero for every later restoration. Practice questions often treat zero point zero four as the rule for every restoration, or claim zero applies even the first time. Neither is right. There is also a second source of confusion. Zero point zero four is the same number as the commercial per se limit, but the two rules are unrelated: one is a restriction on a restored license, the other is the DWI limit for commercial drivers. Read which rule the question is asking about.

title.text: When the restriction starts at zero

lines.text: Driving under twenty-one after drinking or drugs.

narration.text: For some convictions, the restriction is zero point zero zero from the very first restoration. That applies after a DWI conviction in a commercial motor vehicle, a conviction for driving under twenty-one after consuming alcohol or drugs, or a conviction for felony death by vehicle. These cases share a theme: either the driver was in a vehicle held to a higher standard, the driver was too young to be drinking at all, or someone died. For these drivers, the law skips the zero point zero four step and sets zero tolerance from the start.

lines.text: Interlock: BAC point one five or more.
Or another conviction in seven years.
Seizure if convicted while revoked for DWI.

narration.text: A DWI conviction with a BAC of zero point one five or more, or with another conviction in the past seven years, requires an ignition interlock device on the vehicle. The interlock tests the driver's breath and blocks the engine from starting if alcohol is detected. Notice that its seven-year window needs only one prior, while the fourth-offense felony rule needs three priors within seven years. There is a further consequence for the most serious repeat cases. If you are convicted of DWI while already revoked for an earlier DWI, the court may order your vehicle seized and sold.

Here is a quick check: Morgan has had two DWI suspensions, and the license is now being restored for the second time. Morgan is an adult driving an ordinary car. What BAC restriction applies to the restored license? Work it out before reading on. The answer is zero point zero zero. Only the first restoration allows zero point zero four, and every later restoration is set at zero. If Morgan's conviction had also involved a BAC of zero point one five or more, or another conviction within seven years, an ignition interlock device would be required on the vehicle as well.

lines.text: Interlock for high BAC or a recent prior.

narration.text: Let us recap. A BAC restriction is placed on a license restored after a DWI suspension or on a limited privilege after a DWI conviction. It is zero point zero four on the first restoration and zero point zero zero on every later one, and it starts at zero after a commercial-vehicle DWI, an under-twenty-one alcohol or drug conviction, or felony death by vehicle. A BAC of zero point one five or more, or another conviction in seven years, requires an ignition interlock. And a DWI conviction while revoked for DWI can lead to vehicle seizure and sale.

why_how.text: The legal age to buy alcohol is twenty-one, and the state uses license revocation to enforce it.
Adults who help underage drinkers share the blame, so they face the same revocation.
Young drivers face an any-amount rule, because even small amounts of alcohol raise crash risk for inexperienced drivers.

scenario.text: Jamie, age twenty-two, lets a nineteen-year-old cousin use Jamie's license to buy beer.

reasoning.text: The cousin faces a one-year revocation for using someone else's ID, and Jamie faces a one-year revocation for letting the cousin use it.

result.text: Both lose their licenses for a year if convicted, because the helper faces the same penalty as the underage buyer.

claim.text: Many people think an adult who helps an underage buyer gets off lightly because the adult is of legal age.

correction.text: An adult who lends an ID or gives alcohol to an underage person faces the same one-year revocation as the underage buyer.

prompt.text: Jamie, twenty-two, lends a license to a nineteen-year-old cousin who buys beer. If both are convicted, what does Jamie face?

answer.text: A one-year license revocation, the same as the cousin.

rationale.text: Letting an underage person use your ID to buy alcohol carries the same one-year revocation as the underage offense.

narration.text: This lesson covers the alcohol laws aimed at people under twenty-one, and at the adults around them. North Carolina sets the legal age to buy alcohol at twenty-one and uses driver license revocation as a main enforcement tool, even for offenses that happen in a store rather than on the road. You will learn the penalties for underage buying, for using fake or borrowed identification, and for adults who lend identification or give alcohol to someone underage. Then you will see the strict any-amount rule that applies to drivers under twenty-one behind the wheel.

The legal age to buy any alcoholic beverage in North Carolina is twenty-one, and anyone younger who buys or tries to buy alcohol breaks the law. The penalty reaches the driver license. An underage person convicted of buying or trying to buy alcohol, or of helping another underage person do so, faces a one-year license revocation. Notice the word trying. A failed attempt at the register still counts. And helping a friend who is also underage counts too. So the revocation can follow from a store purchase that never involved driving at all.

lines.text: Using a fake ID: one year.
Using someone else's ID: one year.

narration.text: Identification is the other common route. An underage person convicted of using, or trying to use, a fake license or ID, or someone else's license or ID, to get alcohol faces a one-year revocation. The penalty does not stop with the underage person. Any person convicted of letting an underage person use their license or ID to buy alcohol, or of giving alcohol to an underage person, also faces a one-year revocation. So lending a license to a younger sibling or friend puts the lender's own license on the line, even if the lender is well over twenty-one.

Here is the trap. Many learners assume an adult who helps an underage drinker faces a lighter penalty, or none, because the adult is of legal drinking age. That is wrong. An adult who lends an ID to an underage buyer, or gives alcohol to an underage person, faces the same one-year revocation as the underage buyer. On practice questions, reject options that say the adult faces nothing, a warning, or a shorter revocation. The memory line is short: same year for helpers. Both sides of the transaction risk the same loss of driving privileges.

lines.text: Any alcohol or drugs in the body.
Not measured against the adult limit.

narration.text: Behind the wheel, drivers under twenty-one face the strictest rule of all. A driver under twenty-one convicted of driving with any amount of alcohol or drugs in their body loses their license for one year. Any amount means exactly that: there is no small allowance, and the adult per se BAC limit does not protect a young driver. Drivers under twenty-one face an any-amount rule with a one-year revocation, unlike adults, who are measured against the per se BAC limit. So for anyone under twenty-one, the only legal amount of alcohol in the body while driving is none.

lines.text: Cousin is nineteen and buys beer.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Jamie is twenty-two and lends a driver license to a nineteen-year-old cousin, who uses it to buy beer. Both are later convicted. What does Jamie face? Work it out before reading on. The answer is a one-year license revocation, the same as the cousin. Letting an underage person use your ID to buy alcohol carries the same one-year revocation as the underage offense of using someone else's ID. Being over twenty-one does not protect Jamie. Both licenses are lost for a year, even though nobody was driving during the purchase.

lines.text: Buyers, fake IDs and helpers: one year.
Under twenty-one: any amount costs a year.

narration.text: To wrap up, the legal age to buy alcohol in North Carolina is twenty-one. An underage person convicted of buying or trying to buy alcohol, helping another underage person do so, or using a fake or borrowed ID faces a one-year revocation. An adult convicted of lending an ID to an underage buyer or giving alcohol to an underage person faces the same one-year revocation. And a driver under twenty-one convicted of driving with any amount of alcohol or drugs in the body loses the license for one year, because young drivers face an any-amount rule rather than the adult limit.
